clue.text: (see 11ac.)
Blow job in essence means removing a nut

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it goes inside it

parts.note: one's being is one's essential nature
crude slang for oral sex

explanation.surface: A crude claim that oral sex can somehow lead to castration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' is slang for the head, so 'removing a nut' is decapitation, not anything sexual.
explanation.definitionFit: Nut is British slang for the head, so taking off someone's nut is decapitation.

clue.text: Freddie's pet dish showing a bit of thigh, having rest after being screwed?

parts.words: dish showing a bit of thigh
parts.note: ham is a dish cut from the pig's thigh

indicators.note: something screwed is twisted round, so these letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A risqué dinner-party scene: thigh on show, a lie-down after sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freddie Starr Ate My Hamster' was a famous 1986 front page of The Sun about the British comedian.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabloid legend made a hamster the comedian Freddie Starr's supposed snack, so the pet is linked to him.

clue.text: PC attacker game to be gobbled by short noble

indicators.note: what is gobbled ends up inside the eater, so one piece is swallowed within the other

parts.note: Vis. is the short form of viscount
rugby union

explanation.surface: A political-correctness zealot's game being swallowed up by a minor aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PC' looks like political correctness, as elsewhere in this puzzle, but here it is a personal computer.
explanation.definitionFit: A computer virus is malicious code that infects and damages a personal computer.

clue.text: Is in opposition, so thing comes to point

indicators.note: one thing coming to another arrives next to it, so the two pieces are joined end to end

parts.note: an object is a thing
south, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: An argument where the opposition's position reaches its crux.
explanation.definitionFit: To object is to express opposition, so someone who objects is against the proposal.

clue.text: Teresa and head of Theology, writhing, come again

indicators.note: something writhing twists about, so the letters are contorted into another order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A saucy picture of Teresa and a theology don in ecstasy, coming twice.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Come again?' asks someone to repeat what they said, which is to say it once more in the same words.

clue.text: Tumescent like a non-PC homosexual?

parts.note: an old offensive British slang term for a gay man
the suffix -y makes an adjective meaning like or resembling

explanation.surface: A sniggering crude double meaning about swelling.
explanation.walkthrough: Puff, or poof, is dated offensive British slang, hence 'non-PC'.
explanation.definitionFit: Puffy means swollen, the same as tumescent, which describes tissue that has puffed up.

clue.text: (see 23dn.)
Something for addicts of blow job equipment and clobber

parts.note: a fan's job is to blow air
to clobber is to hit, as with a club

explanation.surface: Paraphernalia for cocaine users and for oral sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' is slang for cocaine and 'clobber' British slang for clothes, but here the blowing is a fan's and clobbering is hitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Fans are devotees or enthusiasts, hooked on a star, and a fan club is the organisation for them.

clue.text: Hey-hey! Sadie's top keeps going up and down!

parts.note: yo is a casual greeting, twice

indicators.note: the top of a down entry's word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: An excited cry about Sadie's top bouncing about.
explanation.definitionFit: To yo-yo is to fluctuate repeatedly, moving up and down like the spinning toy on its string.

clue.text: Simpson gets order to penetrate hot Brenda

indicators.note: to penetrate is to go into, so one piece is pushed inside the others

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot on taps
the Order of Merit
Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER

explanation.surface: A Simpson is told to have sex with a randy woman called Brenda.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye has long called Queen Elizabeth 'Brenda', so Brenda stands for her ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer is the father in the cartoon family The Simpsons.

clue.text: Imagine very recently coupling with Caprice …

parts.note: as in 'it has just happened'
a passing whim or caprice is a fancy

explanation.surface: Gossip that someone has just slept with the model Caprice.
explanation.walkthrough: Caprice Bourret was a much-photographed model of the 1990s, so the capital disguises an ordinary noun.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Just fancy!' is an exclamation of surprise meaning 'imagine that!'

clue.text: (& 1ac./25dn.) "Oh — Saudi overreaction!" — Blair, spinning government measure to deal with delinquency

definitions.text: government measure to deal with delinquency

indicators.note: a spin-doctor twists words, and spinning letters round leaves them in a new order

parts.note: the exclamation plus the Prime Minister's name, every letter used

explanation.surface: Tony Blair's spin machine dismisses a Saudi protest as an overreaction.
explanation.walkthrough: All 24 letters of the quotation and 'Blair' are rearranged into the three linked lights. Blair's government brought in the ASBO in 1998.
explanation.definitionFit: The ASBO was a civil court order introduced by Blair's Labour government to curb nuisance and petty crime by youths.

clue.text: Extra! Andrew Motion briefly takes on Private Eye!

indicators.note: taking something on means adding it, so the second piece is attached after the first

parts.note: Motion was Poet Laureate, abbreviated PL
the magazine speaking of itself

explanation.surface: A newspaper bill announcing the Poet Laureate's attack on Private Eye.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Motion was Britain's Poet Laureate from 1999 to 2009; the magazine setting this puzzle is 'us'.
explanation.definitionFit: Plus means in addition, so something extra is a plus.

clue.text: Islamic sect quiet over Iraq, oddly

parts.note: the call for silence

indicators.note: only the odd-numbered letters, first and third, are kept

parts.note: first and third letters of the country's name

explanation.surface: A news report on a Muslim sect lying low in Iraq.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' places one piece above the next.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shia are one of the two main branches of Islam, strong in Iraq and Iran.

clue.text: Decrepit Iris cavorting with nun

indicators.note: to cavort is to leap about wildly, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An ageing Iris frolicking with a nun.
explanation.definitionFit: A building in ruins is falling apart, which is what decrepit means.

clue.text: (see 26dn.)
Show shagging doesn't start with Hello! piece

indicators.note: a word that does not start has lost its opening letter

parts.note: British slang for having sex
a greeting
a bit is a piece

explanation.surface: A TV show where the sex never gets going, alongside a piece in Hello! magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Hello! is a celebrity magazine, but here it is just a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhibit something is to put it on display, to show it.

clue.text: Perhaps Polo Mint's last given to one getting knickers in a twist?

indicators.note: the last letter of the word is the one kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

parts.words: one getting knickers in a twist
parts.note: one who ravels tangles things

explanation.surface: A Polo mint handed to someone who is all worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: Polo is the British mint with a hole, but here it is Marco Polo; 'perhaps' marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Marco Polo, the Venetian explorer who reached China, is a famous example of a traveller.

clue.text: Stick with froth as an oral irritation

parts.note: gum is glue, used to stick
a liquid froths when it boils

explanation.surface: A rude hint about something sticky and frothy irritating the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: A gumboil is a painful abscess on the gum, an irritation inside the mouth.

clue.text: Strong-smelling substance, "arse fur"

parts.note: surface reading: a smelly substance described crudely as hair from the backside
setter's reading: an animal named for the musky secretion from glands at its rear, and prized for its pelt

explanation.walkthrough: The muskrat is an American water rodent; its scent glands lie near the tail, and its fur is traded as musquash. The clue's exact wordplay is uncertain.
explanation.definitionFit: The rodent's name joins the strong-smelling musk it secretes to its rat-like body, and its pelt is a commercial fur.

clue.text: They could go to a victor's head (Bush's)

definitions.text: They could go to a victor's head (Bush's)

parts.words: They could go to a victor's head (Bush's)
parts.note: surface reading: success going to the winner's head, George W. Bush's in particular

parts.words: They could go to a victor's head (Bush's)
parts.note: setter's reading: leaves from a bush, woven into a winner's wreath

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush's' points to the President, but the leaves really are a bush's; Bush's wife Laura adds a further pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient victors were crowned with a wreath of leaves from the bay tree, hence resting on one's laurels.

clue.text: City bird's taken to drink

parts.note: a large water bird
'the drink' is slang for the sea

explanation.surface: A city girl has taken to the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' suggests a woman and 'drink' alcohol; Swansea is a city on the south coast of Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Swansea is a Welsh coastal city that was granted city status in 1969.

clue.text: On leave, starts to uplift and pad bust

parts.note: to split is slang for to leave

indicators.note: the starts of the following words are their first letters

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Off duty, a woman starts lifting and padding out her bra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uplift', 'pad' and 'bust' all suggest lingerie; 'bust' is really the verb, as in a couple busting up.
explanation.definitionFit: Couples who bust up separate, so bust means to end a relationship.

clue.text: Government-style gloss on events not allowed to prolong its life?

parts.note: political spin puts a favourable gloss on news
as in a ruling that something is out

explanation.surface: A jibe that a government lives by spin to keep itself in office.
explanation.definitionFit: To spin something out is to make it last longer, stretching its life.

clue.text: Writer without pair to thrust out

indicators.note: without means lacking, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: Marcel Proust, the French novelist
the standard abbreviation for pair

explanation.surface: A writer with no partner is pushed aside.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust someone is to expel them or force them out of a position.

clue.text: (& 6d.) Breathless, openly gay, related to a derisory gay

parts.note: someone who is out is open about being gay
of means belonging or related to
an old offensive British slang term for a gay man

explanation.surface: A gasping description of a gay man linked to a homophobic insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out of puff is the British idiom for having run out of breath.

clue.text: Gordon's prime, universal evil: "Tone moving without one to cut short parliamentary debate" …

indicators.note: without means outside, so the letters go round the next piece
the prime or foremost part of the name is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

indicators.note: letters that are moving shift out of their order

parts.note: the film certificate for all ages
ill means harm or evil
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown's camp says Tony Blair is moving to stifle debate in the Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon is Brown and 'Tone' is Tony Blair, but both are only letter sources. TONE is rearranged around I.
explanation.definitionFit: In Parliament the guillotine is a timetable motion that forces a vote by cutting debate short; as a verb it means to curtail that debate.

clue.text: (see 11ac.)
(& 15d.) Do what a younger Schwarzenegger did: act like a wanker — smooth!

definitions.text: Do what a younger Schwarzenegger did

parts.note: a crude reference to the pumping hand action
to iron clothes is to smooth them

explanation.surface: A jeer at a young muscleman as a tosser with a smooth body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanker' is British slang for a masturbator, and also a general insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Before Hollywood, Arnold Schwarzenegger was a champion bodybuilder, and pumping iron is lifting weights; it was also his 1977 film's title.

clue.text: … raging: "Endless shit, endless bollocks, little entertainment!"

indicators.note: with no end, the final letter of the word is cut away

parts.note: a lump of excrement

indicators.note: again the last letter of the following word is removed

parts.note: both mean nonsense

indicators.note: a little version of a word is its short form, keeping only its start

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A furious critic dismisses a show as endless rubbish with little entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ent' is short for entertainment. The opening dots carry on from the 24-across rant.
explanation.definitionFit: Raging and turbulent both describe something violently stormy and wild, like a raging or turbulent sea.

clue.text: Lord Owen's first drunken slobber

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so these letters lurch out of order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: only the first letter of the name is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: Lord David Owen, the former Foreign Secretary, slobbering when drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: To drool is to let saliva dribble from the mouth, the same as slobbering.

clue.text: Suit, old West Midlands Police style?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to equip or kit out
second meaning: a frame-up with planted or invented evidence

explanation.walkthrough: The West Midlands Serious Crime Squad was disbanded in 1989 after it was found to have faked evidence and confessions.
explanation.definitionFit: A fit-up is British slang for framing an innocent person, and to fit up a place is to furnish or equip it.

clue.text: High-ranking cops smear A-list celeb

parts.note: superintendents, senior police officers
to tar someone is to smear their name

explanation.surface: Senior police officers trying to smear a celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: A superstar is a hugely famous performer, the top tier of celebrity known as the A-list.
